\chapter{In the Kitchen}
\label{ch:te-kitchen}
\hlchaptermodality{61}

\begin{chapteropening}

\section[perugu]{\te{పెరుగు} (perugu) — curd}

\label{lesson:TE-C61-curd}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pakṣi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పెరుగు}}
\textbf{\te{పెరుగు}} (\emph{perugu}) — \textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పెరుగు} is set curd: \te{పాలు} left overnight with a spoonful of yesterday's \te{పెరుగు} stirred in. It closes almost every meal in a Telugu house, and a \emph{bhōjanaṁ} without it is thought unfinished.

The word is inherited, and Telugu uses the same shape for what curd does and for what anything does when it grows. Curd is milk that grew.

A \te{గేదె}'s \te{పాలు} set thicker than a cow's, which is one reason a village that keeps buffaloes is in no hurry to change.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first thing in the kitchen.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{perugu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{perugu}, then \emph{pālu}, and say which one comes first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పెరుగు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[neyyi]{\te{నెయ్యి} (neyyi) — ghee}

\label{lesson:TE-C61-ghee}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{perugu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నెయ్యి}}
\textbf{\te{నెయ్యి}} (\emph{neyyi}) — \textquotedblleft{}ghee\textquotedblright{}.

\te{నెయ్యి} is clarified butter, and it is what \te{పెరుగు} becomes after churning and heating. Three things out of one: \te{పాలు}, \te{పెరుగు}, \te{నెయ్యి}.

The word is inherited and very old. Its root runs across the whole family for the same fat, which suits a food that has been made the same way for longer than any of these languages have been separate.

A spoonful of \te{నెయ్యి} over rice is both a taste and a courtesy. It is what a house puts in front of an \emph{atithi} first.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and the second is made out of the first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{neyyi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{neyyi}, then \emph{perugu}, and say which one is poured
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నెయ్యి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}ghee\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nūne]{\te{నూనె} (nūne) — oil}

\label{lesson:TE-C61-oil}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{neyyi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నూనె}}
\textbf{\te{నూనె}} (\emph{nūne}) — \textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.

\te{నూనె} is oil pressed from seeds — groundnut, sesame, sunflower — and it is what a kitchen cooks with on the days it is not cooking with \te{నెయ్యి}.

The word is inherited, and Telugu keeps it firmly apart from \te{నెయ్యి}. One comes from an animal and one comes from a \te{విత్తనం}, and no cook mixes the two up.

\te{నూనె} also works outside the kitchen. It is what goes into a \te{దీపం}, and a house that has run out of it sits in the dark.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nūne}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nūne}, then \emph{neyyi}, and say which one a \te{దీపం} takes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నూనె} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cakkera]{\te{చక్కెర} (cakkera) — sugar}

\label{lesson:TE-C61-sugar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nūne} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చక్కెర}}
\textbf{\te{చక్కెర}} (\emph{cakkera}) — \textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.

\te{చక్కెర} is sugar, and the word is a traveller. Sanskrit \emph{śarkarā} meant \textquotedblleft{}grit, gravel\textquotedblright{} — the stuff arrived in grains — and the same word went west through Persian and Arabic and Latin until English got \textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{} out of it. The Telugu shape and the English one are cousins with a very long road between them.

Telugu also keeps \te{బెల్లం}, the unrefined block of palm or cane sugar, for everything traditional. \te{చక్కెర} is the white refined thing that came later.

A pinch of \te{చక్కెర} goes into dishes an English kitchen would leave savoury, and it goes in to round off the salt rather than to make anything sweet.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cakkera}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{cakkera}, then \emph{perugu}, and say which one is stirred into the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చక్కెర} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mirapa]{\te{మిరప} (mirapa) — a chilli}

\label{lesson:TE-C61-chilli}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cakkera} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మిరప}}
\textbf{\te{మిరప}} (\emph{mirapa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a chilli\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మిరప} is the chilli, and it is the newest thing in this kitchen by several thousand years. The plant crossed from the Americas on Portuguese ships and reached the coast about four hundred years ago.

The word is older than the plant it names. It belonged to black pepper first, and when the new pod arrived and took over the job of making food hot, the name went with the job rather than staying with the plant.

Andhra cooking is built on it now, and a kitchen there measures itself by how much \te{మిరప} it can carry. Five things, and the person at the stove will ask your \te{పేరు} before the meal is over.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{పెరుగు}, \te{నెయ్యి}, \te{నూనె}, \te{చక్కెర}, \te{మిరప}. Enough to name what a kitchen holds while somebody asks you your \te{పేరు}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mirapa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say \emph{nā pēru} and your own name
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మిరప} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a chilli\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
